**Monday, February 29, 1960**

Before anything else: you share your birthday with a day that doesn't exist most years. February 29 comes around once every four years — or more precisely, three times every twelve years, skipping century years not divisible by 400. By the calendar you were born under, you have turned 66 years old. But you have seen only sixteen actual February 29 birthdays since your first one. Most years your birthday simply isn't there. You were born into a kind of calendrical rarity that no other date carries: not just a day in history, but a day that history usually skips.

---

**The day itself**

On February 29, 1960, an earthquake struck the Moroccan city of Agadir just after midnight. It was a relatively modest magnitude — roughly 5.7 — but it was catastrophically shallow, rupturing only a few kilometers beneath the surface, directly under one of the city's most densely populated quarters. In seconds, large portions of Agadir collapsed. Between twelve and fifteen thousand people died, in a city of roughly thirty thousand. It was one of the deadliest natural disasters in North African history, and it reshaped how engineers thought about building codes and seismic hazard in cities sitting atop faults they'd underestimated. You were born on the same day a city was nearly erased.

---

**Twenty years earlier, to the day**

On February 29, 1940 — exactly twenty years before your birth — the twelfth Academy Awards ceremony was held in Los Angeles. Hattie McDaniel won Best Supporting Actress for her role in *Gone with the Wind*, becoming the first Black person to win an Academy Award. She was not permitted to sit with her castmates at the ceremony. She was seated at a segregated table at the back of the room, separated from the rest of the production's team by the policies of the venue. She accepted the award with a short, gracious speech and returned to her table.

Two decades later, twenty-eight days before you were born, four Black college students sat down at the Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina and refused to leave when they were denied service. Within weeks, sit-ins had spread to dozens of cities across the South. The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee was founded that April. The world you arrived into was one where the distance between Hattie McDaniel's segregated table and the Greensboro counter had not yet been crossed — but people were crossing it.

---

**The year itself**

1960 is sometimes called "The Year of Africa." Seventeen African nations gained independence that year — Senegal, Mali, Ivory Coast, Nigeria, Cameroon, Congo, Niger, Chad, and others — as the European colonial map drawn in the nineteenth century was torn up with remarkable speed. The world map looked measurably different at the end of 1960 than it had at the start. You were born into a moment of global political transformation that future historians would regard as one of the fastest reshapings of sovereignty in recorded history.

In the United States, you were born in the final year of the Eisenhower presidency. John F. Kennedy would be elected president in November, eight months after your birth. The decade that followed — shaped by Kennedy, then Johnson, then Nixon, by Vietnam and the moon landing and the assassinations and the upheaval — would form the backdrop of your childhood and adolescence. You were nine when Armstrong stepped off the ladder. You were twelve when the last Apollo mission left the Moon, and no human has been back since.

The FDA approved the birth control pill in May 1960, three months after you were born. The transformation that followed — in women's autonomy, in family structure, in the workforce, in the entire social architecture of the second half of the twentieth century — was set in motion the same year you arrived.

---

**The arc**

You are 66 now. You were born the same year the first working laser was demonstrated, the same year the U-2 spy plane was shot down over the Soviet Union and turned the Cold War sharply colder. Television had arrived but was still in black and white for most households. A long-distance phone call required an operator. A computer was something a government or university owned, not a person.

Over the decades: the civil rights legislation of the mid-1960s, Vietnam, Watergate, the fall of Saigon, personal computers, AIDS, the fall of the Berlin Wall, the internet, 9/11, the smartphone, the sequencing of the human genome, and now artificial intelligence rewriting what it means to do knowledge work. The Greensboro lunch counter where those four students sat twenty-eight days before your birth is now a museum.

And through all of it, you've marked time by a calendar that mostly ignores your actual birthday. Sixty-six years, seventeen February 29s. The world has spun on its axis roughly 24,000 times since you arrived on the one day in four years that most people treat as a curiosity. You have lived it as a life.
